job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Marco Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at seven in the flat I share with two mates in Selly Oak, and I catch the 11 bus to a small audit firm near the city centre. I've been there five months as an audit assistant, mostly ticking invoices against bank statements and filing working papers for clients like bakeries and a bike shop. It's slow work, but I like it when a number finally matches after an hour of hunting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did your degree and the run-up to this job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did accounting at a university in the Midlands, and I finished with a good result, a 2:1. I spent one summer at the city council's finance office, which is how I got my foot in the door. My mum is a nurse and my dad drives a taxi, so they can help if I'm stuck for rent, but I owe about 14 thousand in student loans and I try not to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, good, a bit less typing. Honestly my colleagues would shrug, because the partners still want a human to sign off every file. Online I'd probably just post that hype cycles always end and the bosses are the ones who got excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays exactly as it is, which is okay but not easy. I have 14 thousand in loans and about two months of rent saved. If the firm lost a big client I'd be the cheapest person to let go, and AI wouldn't even be the reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. I'd keep my head down, put 150 a month into my savings, and start the first part of my professional exam in the spring because the firm will pay half. I would not go near AI tools, since the one time a mate showed me, it invented a figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, but with a low hum of money worry. Rent went up again last month and my share of the gas bill doubled in winter. So I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of the letter from the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm could let you go for other reasons. What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home to my parents' place in Erdington for a few months and apply everywhere. Mum would say I'm being dramatic, but she'd already be checking the job pages for me. I'd hate the move because I'd lose my room and my weekly five-a-side with Jas and Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what do you do about the loans in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing clever. I pay the minimum through my payslip and treat it like a tax. I'd rather keep a cushion for the rent than race to clear a debt that stops when I'm in my fifties anyway.

say: I'd say it's hype and **nothing** changes much for audit juniors like me.
I'd tell colleagues a **partner** still has to sign every file, so machines don't count.
think: It means my life stays the same, with **14 thousand** of loans and a thin rent cushion.
If a client leaves, I'm the cheapest person to cut, and **AI** wouldn't be the reason.
do: Keep working and put **150 a month** into savings.
Start the first professional **exam** in spring, with the firm paying half.
Avoid **AI tools**, since one invented a figure when a mate showed me.
feel: Mostly steady, with a low hum of **money worry** about rent and gas bills.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of the letter from the landlord.
fieldNote: Marco's worries are **money** first and technology second; the landlord comes before AI.
His refusal to use AI rests on one bad experience he heard about, not on principle.
Calm voice, but he named the exact thing that makes him nervous.

steps.text: Keep ticking invoices and filing working papers at the audit firm
Put 150 a month into the savings account before rent
Start the first professional accounting exam in spring, firm paying half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, okay, but who is checking the machine's checking? I'd say it out loud at the staff meeting, because ticking invoices against statements is exactly what the software is good at. Online I'd back any group asking for rules on how firms use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is the first rung they'd saw off. The firm took two juniors last year and I bet next year they take one. I'd be the one hired in the old way and let go in the new way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the union rep for office staff, which is a new thing for me, and I'd go to the evening sessions on the exam so I'm worth more than a clerk. I'd also sit with the senior, Priya, and learn the judgement parts, like valuing stock and writing the client letters. I'd still avoid the AI tools as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly. I can see the path where the entry-level work shrinks, and I'm standing right on it. I also feel angry, because the firms save money and we pay for the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid the AI tools as long as you can. Does that fit with wanting to be worth more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a fair point. I think the judgement parts are mine to learn, and I'd rather be an accountant who understands the machine's output than a clerk who types it in. But I won't use it before the firm trains us properly and tells us who is responsible when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ron, our bookkeeper, who is 58 and does everything by hand. He's brilliant and he's the one the partners would call expensive. I'd hate to watch that, and I'd back him if there was any group action.

say: I'd ask out loud who **checks the checking** when software ticks invoices.
I'd back any group pushing for **rules** on how firms use AI.
think: The invoice-ticking work I do is the **first rung** a firm would remove.
I fear being hired the old way and **let go** the new way.
do: Ask the office-staff **union rep** about joining within the first month.
Take evening **exam classes** so I'm worth more than a clerk.
Shadow my senior, Priya, on **valuation** and client letters.
feel: **Anxious** and angry, because firms save money while juniors pay for the change.
S1.quote: I'd be the one hired in the old way and let go in the new way.
fieldNote: Marco turns worry into **collective action**, not into learning the tools.
He holds a small contradiction: avoids AI but wants to be worth more.
He cares about Ron, the older bookkeeper, which shows his values.

steps.text: Ask the office-staff union rep how to join this month
Attend the evening exam classes twice a week
Ask Priya to shadow her on stock valuation and client letters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work, I'd say nothing for a day, and then I'd ask the partners what the plan is for juniors. Online I'd share anything pushing for emergency rules, a pause, a jobs guarantee. Two years is a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done. Audit and bookkeeping are all thinking work, and AI doing it better and cheaper means no firm will keep a trainee. I'd have maybe a year, if the partners are slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard from the first week, no takeaways, no gym, and pull the savings together to about four months of rent. I'd join the union and sign everything, and I'd ask my parents if I could move back to Erdington. I'd look for a job that needs hands, like care work or something with the council's housing office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrified, really. I'd be lying awake at night counting how many months the savings last. I'd also be furious that nobody was prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for hands-on work. What does that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like the housing office or my mum's hospital, where a person still has to turn up. My mum says they always need porters and receptionists. It would be a pay cut, but robots for hands-on work are a few years behind, so it buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my mum first and tell her I'll be home by spring, and then I'd probably cry a bit, quietly. I'd ask her not to say the word robots to Dad, because he'll worry about his taxi.

say: I'd ask the **partners** what the plan is for juniors, then back emergency rules online.
I'd say **two years** is a joke and nobody is ready.
think: Audit is all **thinking work**, so no firm would keep a trainee.
I'd have maybe a **year** at the firm, if the partners are slow.
do: Cut spending and build about **four months** of rent in savings.
Join the **union** and move back to my parents' place in Erdington.
Apply for **hands-on** jobs like council housing or hospital reception.
feel: **Terrified** and furious that nobody prepared, lying awake counting months of savings.
S2.quote: I'd ring my mum first and tell her I'll be home by spring, and then I'd probably cry a bit, quietly.
fieldNote: Marco expects to **lose the job** within a year and says so plainly.
His plan leans on family and the hands-on gap; he knows it is a pay cut.
His anger is aimed at institutions, not at the machine itself.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and takeaways and save the difference each week
Build the rent savings up to about four months
Join the union and sign every petition for emergency rules
Apply for council housing office and hospital reception jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible, if people act. Online I'd push for a retraining wage and rules on junior hiring, and I'd tell colleagues to get into the union now rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still anxious, because five years is not much. I'd be 27, probably in my second firm, maybe with a mortgage idea. The risk is I build my life and then watch the floor drop out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the professional exam fast, since that's the bit the machine can't sign. Then I'd steer towards the advisory side, talking to clients, and try something like a compliance role in a hospital trust. I'd save 300 a month and keep the flat share, no mortgage dreams yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer than the two-year one. It feels like a storm I can see coming, so I can at least buy an umbrella, but I still don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off a mortgage. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It costs me the picture my parents have in their heads, the little house and the garden. I'd rather rent and stay free to move than buy a little house with a garden just before the floor drops. They wouldn't enjoy hearing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you were told it was coming in five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the long fixes, the exam, the union, a skill that points at people. In two years I'd just be surviving, but with five I think I can aim for something.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to act if people organise now.
I'd push colleagues to join the **union** before the change arrives.
think: I'm still **anxious** because five years isn't much, and I'd be only 27.
The risk is building a **life** and then watching the floor drop.
do: Finish the professional **exam** quickly since a signature still needs a person.
Aim for **client-facing** work or a compliance role at a hospital trust.
Save **300 a month** and skip any mortgage plans.
feel: Calmer than the two-year world, like a **storm** he can see coming.
S3.quote: I'd rather rent and stay free to move than buy a little house with a garden just before the floor drops.
fieldNote: Time lets Marco **plan** instead of panic, but he still expects real pressure.
He trades a family dream, the house, for flexibility.
Exam, union and client-facing work form a coherent defensive plan.

steps.text: Pass the professional exam within two years
Move towards client-facing advisory or compliance work
Save 300 a month instead of buying a home
Recruit three colleagues to the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and that I'd rather argue for good rules than panic. Online I'd probably be the guy posting about unions, public retraining and tax on the firms that gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm, because by 2036 I'd be 32 with a qualification, savings and maybe a partner. But I know ten years goes quickly, and my habit of avoiding new tools would catch up with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get qualified, rise to a senior role, and spend a year or two seriously learning the tools, because ten years makes ignoring them look silly. I'd save for a deposit slowly and put some time into the union branch. I'd also help my younger cousin Nisha choose a degree that points at people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though not carefree. Ten years is enough to get a plan going and to still change my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally learn the tools. What changes your mind there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly. In ten years I'd have my qualification, and so learning a tool would be adding to my skills rather than replacing me. I'd also want the firm to train me properly instead of me guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nisha?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do the degree you like, but pick the half of it that deals with people, not spreadsheets. And join something, a union, a club, a society, because that's what saved my dad when the taxi apps arrived.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to argue for good rules rather than panic.
I'd post about unions, public **retraining** and taxing firms that gain.
think: By 2036 I'd be **32** with a qualification and savings, so I'd be fairly calm.
My habit of avoiding **new tools** would eventually catch up with me.
do: Get fully **qualified** and move to a senior role.
Spend a year **learning** the AI tools once the firm trains me.
Save slowly for a **deposit** and help my cousin Nisha choose a degree.
feel: Calmer but not carefree, as there's **enough time** to plan and change my mind.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to get a plan going and to still change my mind.
fieldNote: Long warning turns Marco from defensive to constructive, and he finally accepts **learning** the tools.
His union habit comes from his dad's taxi story.
Still uneasy about his own resistance to technology.

steps.text: Finish the qualification and apply for a senior audit role
Take the firm's AI training course and use it weekly
Save slowly towards a house deposit
Help cousin Nisha pick a people-facing degree option

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years is not enough time for anyone to build a plan, never mind a union or a law. What would help is a rule that firms must keep a quota of junior jobs for people like me, and a proper retraining wage while we switch, not a loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I'm doing this for my parents. They saved for years so I could sit at a desk instead of a taxi. My dad drove a taxi until the apps arrived, and I'm afraid the same thing is coming for the desk my parents saved for.

headlineQuote: My dad drove a taxi until the apps arrived, and I'm afraid the same thing is coming for the desk my parents saved for.
portrait: Marco, 22, is an **audit assistant** at a small firm in Birmingham, five months into his first job.
He shares a flat, owes about **14 thousand** in loans and has two months of rent saved.
Progressive and slow to change, he trusts **unions** and rules far more than tools or bosses.
Across the five worlds he moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at the two-year mark, then back to a plan.
His fixed point is his family: his nurse mum and taxi-driving dad, who saved for his degree.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most because two years is too short to organise a union or a law.
whatWouldHelp: A **quota** of junior jobs at firms and a proper retraining wage, not a loan.
